findings.text: Per-entry control file write handler. It rejects oversized writes, copies the caller buffer with termination, routes a leading plus command to interpreter binding and otherwise interprets the payload as a management command for disable, enable with first-time publication, or removal, returning the accepted byte count or a negative error.

An entry starts unpublished and configurable, becomes searchable only on enable, and thereafter rejects further configuration. A BPF flavor must be selected before binding, binding is refused once searchable, the first enable inserts the entry exactly once, and removal detaches the dentry so later bind or publish attempts observe absence.

Binding payloads require a plus introducer, a non-empty printable ASCII name without spaces, a single space separator, and an absolute interpreter path consuming the remainder of the write after optional trailing newline stripping. Name length has an upper bound, the total write has a binding length ceiling, and violations report invalid argument while oversize reports too big.

Interpreter file resolution happens before acquiring the filesystem root lock because resolution may reenter the same filesystem. The root lock then serializes the check for concurrent removal or publication against the attach decision, and a separate short spin section protects insertion of the entry into the global search list. Creation-time publication uses the same spin protection.
Per-entry file behavior table provides open, sequential read, custom write, sequential seek and single release handlers, giving a read-evaluate control file abstraction for each registered handler.

Registration creates an exclusive child dentry under the filesystem root, allocates a regular file inode with restricted permissions, links the control structure through private data and operation table, installs the pair persistently, and publishes immediately only when the enabled flag was preset; allocation or name collision failures unwind creation without publishing.

Helper that instantiates a dentry with an inode, marks the dentry persistent with an extra reference, and ensures hash visibility. It warns when asked to instantiate an already positive dentry or a null inode.

Persistent installation acquires the inode lock before the dentry lock, performs instantiation and flag update under both, and rehashes only when currently unhashed. Rehashing itself serializes bucket insertion with the per-bucket lock.

Pair for exclusive creation under a parent directory. The start step validates the name and returns a negative dentry with the parent held; the done step releases the creation hold. Callers must pair them even on inode allocation failure.

Directory operation establishment locks the parent directory for writing, using a killable acquisition in one mode and an uninterruptible nested acquisition in the normal mode, then performs an exclusive component lookup. Lookup failure releases the parent lock and propagates the error pointer; success transfers the held parent to the caller until ended.

Exclusive component resolution first consults the dentry cache, refuses to create under a dead directory, allocates when absent, delegates to the parent filesystem lookup operation, and enforces creation versus exclusivity: missing without create yields not found, present with exclusive yields exists.

Cache lookup returns no entry on miss, otherwise revalidates against the parent inode and flags. Revalidation failure releases the reference and surfaces an error; an explicit zero result additionally invalidates the cached entry before releasing.

Permission-free name preparation hashes the component with the parent as salt, rejects empty names, single and double dot, and any embedded slash or zero byte, then optionally consults a filesystem supplied hash operation when the parent advertises it.

Two build variants provide salted full-name hashing and salted hash-plus-length computation over zero-terminated or counted inputs. One variant processes word sized chunks with mixing and masked tails, the other iterates byte wise from an initial salted state to a final folded value.

Global register file write handler. It builds a control structure from the caller payload, resolves a named BPF operation set when the BPF flavor is indicated, pre-opens and attaches the interpreter when open-at-register is requested, then installs the entry under the root and transfers ownership to the inode on success.

BPF operation sets are registered per user namespace and selected by exact name match within that namespace. Successful lookup acquires a reference on the operation set before returning; absence or reference failure yields a null result.
The registry list is accessed only with its dedicated spin protection held, using scoped acquisition in the public getter and an assertion of held state in the internal search.

Register file behavior supports only write plus a no-op seek. Status file behavior supports read of a textual flag, write of management commands, and default seeking. Superblock behavior provides filesystem statistics and inode eviction handling.

Status file reports the global enabled flag as a short human readable word followed by newline, using single-copy atomic observation. Writes interpret disable, enable and remove-all commands, updating the flag atomically or purging every entry; unknown commands propagate the parser error.

Bounded buffer read honors the current offset, returns end of data on negative-checked overflow or empty request, truncates the request to remaining bytes, copies to caller space, advances the offset by bytes actually moved, and reports fault only when nothing could be copied.

Filesystem initialization requires the mount user namespace to equal the caller namespace, disables execution and device interpretation and caps stacking depth, lazily allocates a per-namespace control instance exactly once with release ordering, resets the global enabled flag on each mount, builds the initial file tree, and installs super and root directory operations.

Generic in-memory superblock setup assigns page-sized blocks, caller magic, time granularity and default operations, creates a directory root with link count two, then iterates a descriptor table to create regular files with caller modes, sequential numbers and persistent dentries, warning if the table attempts to occupy the reserved root index.

Name-based allocation hashes a zero-terminated component with its parent as salt and allocates a child dentry. Anonymous allocation creates an unparented dentry for a superblock. Root construction combines anonymous allocation with inode instantiation, releasing the inode on allocation failure.

Link count update clears the count through the dedicated clear path when zero is requested, otherwise stores the new value directly and adjusts the superblock removal accounting when transitioning out of zero.

Mount acquisition keys sharing by user namespace, reuses a live matching superblock when namespaces match and exclusivity is not requested, otherwise allocates and publishes a nascent superblock under a global lock. The first creator runs filesystem fill, marks the result active and returns a root reference; fill failure tears down through deactivation, while unused allocations are destroyed without delay.

Superblock discovery and publication serialize on a global lock. Dead instances are skipped via acquire-ordered flag observation, new instances are linked visibly while still nascent for waiters on birth or death, and reference acquisition decides between retry, reuse or busy failure on namespace or exclusivity mismatch.

Concurrent bind, first enable and removal contend on publication state and dentry hashing; the implementation rechecks both after blocking resolution. Additional hazards include creation under a dead directory, name collisions, user namespace mismatch at mount or reuse, exclusive mount refusal, oversized control writes, and negative read offsets.
Maximum accepted binding command length equals the maximum interpreter name length plus the maximum path length plus three delimiter bytes.

Initial tree contains a status file writable by owner and readable by all and a register file writable by owner only, at fixed descriptor positions with root reserved. Root is a directory with conventional permissions, regular entries use restricted permissions, block sizing follows the page size, and mounts carry no-execution and no-device semantics with maximum stacking depth.
